newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - HOLOCAUST CLASS ACTION.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - HOLOCAUST CLASS ACTION.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN
The skill with which insurers such as Allianz and Generali cope with crises is being put to the test with the Holocaust class-action, a case most insurers would never dream of having to face.

A group of Holocaust survivors and their heirs, mostly living in the United States, are bringing a lawsuit for more than $10 billion, claiming the companies owe money on life-insurance policies taken out by those who perished or emigrated during the Nazi period.

The lawyers handling the case say they are now considering expanding the claim, first brought against seven companies two months ago, to include French and Dutch insurers, the Basle and Zurich insurance companies in Switzerland, and another big German insurer, Victoria.
The companies concerned say they have heard nothing official yet.

The issue presents two problems. One is legal. Holocaust victims were, for the most part, paid compensation after the war by the German state. This was meant to cover specific claims (confiscated property, including insurance policies) as well as Germany's' general responsibility for the Nazi genocide.
Officially, the insurers maintain, the matter has therefore been settled.
But the likelihood of this being accepted by an American jury as an end to it all is doubtful.
According to plaintiff's lawyers, there are also signs that the insurers may not have followed Holocaust survivors' inquiries thoroughly enough.

The second battleground is public opinion. Having first tried to play down the story, Allianz has grasped the nettle and is examining its records and allowing University of California history professor Gerald Feldman to study its Nazi-era history.
It has also set up hotline with 30 staff for anyone who believes they might have outstanding claims, although apparently no new cases have emerged.
Allianz also dealt with the potential public relations nightmare of the story it insured Auschwitz by stressing its cooperation with journalists.
But such openness may not help the lawsuit.
The Swiss insurance companies have already contributed Sfr25 million ($17 million) to their country's new Holocaust fund, set up to help untangle the country's banks from their wartime past.

In Italy, Generali, which says it "refuses to recognise any responsibility" in the affair, made a notable concession on June 17, announcing a new $12 million fund for victims of the Holocaust. This also helped Generali push through its commercial expansion plans in Israel.

It will require stamina to defend the action. Sympathy from the jury and the public will be hard to find. There remains a chance the case will ultimately draw in thousands of claimants and more companies.
